Ablation studies confirm the importance of safety-oriented fine-tuning and sentence-level representation for effective feature extraction.
papers.limitation:
Generalization to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness) remains an open question.
Experiments are conducted on relatively small-scale models; evaluation on larger models is needed.
future_direction: Explore the application of SAFER to other alignment dimensions beyond safety (e.g., reasoning, helpfulness).
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a key paradigm for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, yet the reward models at its core remain largely opaque. In this work, we present Sparse Autoencoder For Enhanced Reward model (\textbf{SAFER}), a novel framework for interpreting and improving reward models through mechanistic analysis. Leveraging Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we uncover human-interpretable features in reward model activations, enabling insight into safety-relevant decision-making. We apply SAFER to safety-oriented preference datasets and quantify the salience of individual features by activation differences between chosen and rejected responses. Using these feature-level signals, we design targeted data poisoning and denoising strategies. Experiments show that SAFER can precisely degrade or enhance safety alignment with minimal data modification, without sacrificing general chat performance. Our approach contributes to interpreting, auditing and refining reward models in high-stakes LLM alignment tasks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/xzy-101/SAFER-code. \textit{This paper discusses topics related to reward model safety and may include discussions or examples that highlight potential risks or unsafe outcomes.}

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
Using language-specific features as gating signals to improve steering vectors achieves better control over the language generated by LLMs, with improved performance and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The method does not yet cover certain low-resource languages.
The SAE-based steering vectors sometimes underperform compared to the original steering vectors.
The SAEs used were not trained on curated multilingual data.
future_direction: Utilize language-specific features to guide the training process of multilingual language models.
Investigate low-resource languages to enhance the analysis.
Explore more refined approaches to improve the performance of SAE-based steering vectors.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms behind multilingual capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been examined using neuron-based or internal-activation-based methods. However, these methods often face challenges such as superposition and layer-wise activation variance, which limit their reliability. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer a more nuanced analysis by decomposing the activations of LLMs into a sparse linear combination of SAE features. We introduce a novel metric to assess the monolinguality of features obtained from SAEs, discovering that some features are strongly related to specific languages. Additionally, we show that ablating these SAE features only significantly reduces abilities in one language of LLMs, leaving others almost unaffected. Interestingly, we find some languages have multiple synergistic SAE features, and ablating them together yields greater improvement than ablating individually. Moreover, we leverage these SAE-derived language-specific features to enhance steering vectors, achieving control over the language generated by LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aatrox103/multilingual-llm-features.

papers.title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
papers.research_question: How can we improve the precision and interpretability of activation steering in large language models by leveraging sparse autoencoder features and optimization techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that uses sparse autoencoder features and optimization to construct precise, interpretable steering vectors, improving steering effectiveness and output coherence compared to existing methods.
papers.conclusion: FGAA represents a significant step forward in controlled text generation, offering both theoretical insights into activation patterns and practical advances in steering methodology, while highlighting the trade-off between steering strength and capability preservation.
papers.key_findings:
FGAA outperforms existing activation steering methods (CAA, SAE, SAE-TS) on most steering tasks, especially for the Gemma-2-2B model.
FGAA provides more interpretable steering by operating in the SAE feature space and allowing explicit control over which features are steered.
There is a trade-off between steering strength and preservation of model capabilities: all steering methods degrade model performance (perplexity and benchmark accuracy) at high steering scales.
Negative features in steering vectors tend to degrade steering performance, so FGAA focuses on positive features.
The effectiveness of FGAA varies with model size, showing different performance patterns between Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B.
papers.limitation:
Relies heavily on the quality of feature extraction by the underlying Sparse Autoencoder (SAE).
Optimal selection of n1 and n2 parameters is task-dependent, making universal guidelines challenging.
Developing metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of feature filtering methods is challenging due to the qualitative nature of interpreting features.
future_direction: Investigating how SAE width and quality of SAE features affects steering performance with FGAA.
Exploring techniques to minimize capability degradation at higher steering scales while maintaining steering effectiveness.
Applying FGAA to safety tasks such as controlling sycophancy, hallucination, and refusal in RLHF models and reducing social biases.
papers.abstract: Effective and reliable control over large language model (LLM) behavior is a significant challenge. While activation steering methods, which add steering vectors to a model's hidden states, are a promising approach, existing techniques often lack precision and interpretability in how they influence model outputs. We introduce Feature Guided Activation Additions (FGAA), a novel activation steering method that leverages insights from Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS). By operating in the latent space of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) and employing optimization techniques to select desired SAE features, FGAA constructs precise steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs. In this regard, evaluations on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B models across various steering tasks demonstrate that FGAA outperforms existing steering methods of CAA, SAE decoder steering, and SAE-TS. Our results also highlight important trade-offs between steering scale and general model capabilities that are consistent across all tested steering methods.

papers.title: Enhancing LLM Steering through Sparse Autoencoder-Based Vector Refinement
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors for controlling large language models be refined to be effective when only limited training data is available?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-RSV, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to semantically denoise and augment steering vectors learned from limited data, improving steering performance without model tuning.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RSV is an efficient and interpretable approach for enhancing the steering performance of LLMs with limited training data.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-RSV consistently outperforms all baseline methods, including supervised fine-tuning, across five behavioral concept datasets.
Both the denoising module (removing task-irrelevant features) and the augmentation module (adding missing task-relevant features) contribute to improved steering performance.
Optimal steering performance is achieved with around 15-20 task-relevant features; using too few or too many features degrades performance.
The method is robust to variations in training data size, performing well even with only 10 samples.
The semantics of the selected features align well with the target steering behavior, validating the feature selection approach.
papers.abstract: Steering has emerged as a promising approach in controlling large language models (LLMs) without modifying model parameters. However, most existing steering methods rely on large-scale datasets to learn clear behavioral information, which limits their applicability in many real-world scenarios. The steering vectors extracted from small dataset often contain task-irrelevant noising features, which degrades their effectiveness. To refine the steering vectors learned from limited data, we introduce Refinement of Steering Vector via Sparse Autoencoder (SAE-RSV) that leverages SAEs to semantically denoise and augment the steering vectors. In our framework, we first remove task-irrelevant features according to their semantics provided by SAEs, and then enrich task-relevant features missing from the small dataset through their semantic similarity to the identified relevant features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed SAE-RSV substantially outperforms all the baseline methods including supervised fine-tuning. Our findings show that effective steering vector can be constructed from limited training data by refining the original steering vector through SAEs.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
papers.research_question: How can the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs be reduced while maintaining performance? Specifically, can grouping similar layers and training a single SAE per group achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Group-SAE, a method to reduce the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs by grouping layers with similar residual stream representations and training a single SAE per group, guided by a novel metric called AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance).
papers.conclusion: Group-SAE provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs, achieving significant computational savings without compromising reconstruction quality, downstream task performance, or interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Group-SAE reduces the number of SAEs needed, cutting training costs by up to 50% with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and downstream performance.
The proposed AMAD metric effectively guides the selection of an optimal number of layer groups, balancing efficiency and performance.
Group-SAEs achieve comparable or slightly better interpretability scores (Detection and Fuzzing) than baseline per-layer SAEs.
Features learned by a Group-SAE are most similar to the baseline SAE trained on a layer within its group, and individual features typically peak at a specific layer but spread to adjacent ones.
The method outperforms alternative efficiency baselines like training smaller SAEs on all layers or using evenly spaced groups, especially on downstream performance metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models from the Pythia family trained on the Pile dataset, and the generality to other architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA) or datasets is not evaluated.
The study uses a fixed expansion factor (c=16) and TopK activation function; the impact of these hyperparameter choices is not investigated.
The interpretability evaluation is limited due to the high cost of annotating large numbers of features; a more comprehensive analysis is needed.
future_direction: Further optimizing the number of layer groups and scaling the approach to even larger models.
Evaluating the method on additional datasets and across diverse model architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral).
Conducting a more comprehensive and systematic interpretability analysis.
papers.abstract: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose Group-SAE, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate dictionary learning (sparse autoencoders) for language model interpretability beyond unsupervised proxy metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark with eight metrics to evaluate sparse autoencoders for language model interpretability, and provides an open-source suite of over 200 SAEs for systematic comparison.
papers.conclusion: SAEBench provides a standardized framework for evaluating SAEs, revealing that proxy metrics are insufficient and that different architectures excel at different aspects of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Gains on proxy metrics (sparsity-fidelity) do not reliably translate to better practical performance.
Matryoshka SAEs perform well on feature disentanglement metrics despite underperforming on proxy metrics.
Scaling SAE width has mixed effects: some metrics improve, but feature disentanglement metrics often degrade except for Matryoshka SAEs.
No single sparsity level is optimal for all tasks; moderate sparsity (L0 50-150) offers a reasonable compromise.
ReLU SAEs are outperformed by newer architectures on most metrics.
papers.limitation: The metrics were designed for evaluating SAEs on the same underlying model, not for comparing SAEs across fundamentally different models such as fully trained versus randomly initialized.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular technique for interpreting language model activations, and there is extensive recent work on improving SAE effectiveness. However, most prior work evaluates progress using unsupervised proxy metrics with unclear practical relevance. We introduce SAEBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite that measures SAE performance across eight diverse metrics, spanning interpretability, feature disentanglement and practical applications like unlearning. To enable systematic comparison, we open-source a suite of over 200 SAEs across eight recently proposed SAE architectures and training algorithms. Our evaluation reveals that gains on proxy metrics do not reliably translate to better practical performance. For instance, while Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperform on existing proxy metrics, they substantially outperform other architectures on feature disentanglement metrics; moreover, this advantage grows with SAE scale. By providing a standardized framework for measuring progress in SAE development, SAEBench enables researchers to study scaling trends and make nuanced comparisons between different SAE architectures and training methodologies. Our interactive interface enables researchers to flexibly visualize relationships between metrics across hundreds of open-source SAEs at: www.neuronpedia.org/sae-bench

papers.title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models. It covers technical frameworks, explanation methods, evaluation metrics, and applications.
papers.limitation:
Incomplete Concept Dictionary
Lack Theoretical Foundations
Reconstruction Errors
Computational Burden
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Interpretable LLM Guardrails via Sparse Representation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior to mitigate harmful, misleading, or biased content using sparse representation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SRS, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to disentangle activations into monosemantic features and steer LLM behavior via sparse steering vectors, achieving fine-grained control while preserving output quality.
papers.conclusion: SRS enables precise and interpretable steering of LLM behavior using sparse representations, providing a reliable guardrail for safety, fairness, and truthfulness with superior performance over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRS outperforms existing steering methods like CAA and SAE-TS in single-attribute and multi-attribute control tasks.
SRS maintains high linguistic quality, including grammatical correctness and language diversity, with minimal side effects.
SRS demonstrates robustness against diverse jailbreak prompts, achieving high defense rates.
Multi-attribute control with PCA composition strategy yields the best trade-off between control effectiveness and content quality.
Sparse features enable interpretable identification of attribute-relevant dimensions through KL divergence analysis.
papers.limitation: Multi-attribute steering strategies such as PCA may not fully capture complex relationships and conflicts between attributes.
future_direction: Layer-wise or component-wise multi-attribute steering to align interventions with semantic levels.
Context-aware and personalized steering based on semantic subdomains of prompts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities in generation tasks but are prone to producing harmful, misleading, or biased content, posing significant ethical and safety concerns. To mitigate such risks, representation engineering, which steer model behavior toward desired attributes by injecting carefully designed steering vectors into LLM's representations at inference time, has emerged as a promising alternative to fine-tuning approaches. However, due to the semantically entangled nature of LLM's representation, existing representation engineering methods still suffer from several limitations: limited fine-grained controllability, content quality degradation, and conflict in multi-attribute control. To overcome these challenges, we propose Sparse Representation Steering (SRS), a novel framework that achieves fine-grained and interpretable control over LLM behavior by first disentangling internal activations into a sparse, semantically meaningful representation space, and then selectively steering relevant dimensions. Specifically, SRS leverages a pretrained Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) to transform dense, entangled activation patterns into a sparse monosemantic feature space. To identify relevant features, SRS contrasts sparse activations from positive and negative prompt pairs and measures their bidirectional KL divergence to locate dimensions most associated with the target attribute. We conduct comprehensive experiments on Gemma-2 series model across three alignment dimensions, i.e., safety, fairness, and truthfulness, to evaluate the effectiveness of SRS. Results show that SRS consistently outperforms existing steering methods, which achieves significantly improved controllability across both single and multiple attribute settings, while preserving high linguistic quality and general ability.

papers.title: Jailbreak Antidote: Runtime Safety-Utility Balance via Sparse Representation Adjustment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we balance safety and utility in large language models against jailbreak attacks by adjusting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Jailbreak Antidote, a method for real-time safety-utility balance by sparsely adjusting internal states during inference, showing that safety information is sparsely distributed and adjusting approximately 5% of the state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
papers.conclusion: Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution for real-time safety adjustments in LLMs by directly manipulating internal states, enhancing safety while preserving utility and opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state.
Jailbreak Antidote achieves high defense success rates (DSR) across nine LLMs and ten jailbreak attack methods.
The method preserves model utility, maintaining high Win Rates on AlpacaEval while enhancing safety.
The approach is efficient, introducing negligible computational overhead and no additional token cost during inference.
The safety direction can be identified via PCA on hidden states from benign and harmful prompts.
papers.limitation:
The method requires pre-defined scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k; dynamically adapting these based on context or model confidence could improve flexibility.
Smaller models are inherently limited by their reduced parameter space, which may restrict the extent of safety adjustment.
Developing robust mechanisms to counter adversaries capable of explicitly exploiting the adjustments in internal states remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Dynamically adapting the scaling factor α and sparsity parameter k based on context or model confidence.
Addressing extreme adversarial settings where attackers explicitly exploit the internal state adjustments.
Investigating the applicability of the approach to other aspects of model alignment, such as fairness or domain adaptation.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become integral to various applications, ensuring both their safety and utility is paramount. Jailbreak attacks, which manipulate LLMs into generating harmful content, pose significant challenges to this balance. Existing defenses, such as prompt engineering and safety fine-tuning, often introduce computational overhead, increase inference latency, and lack runtime flexibility. Moreover, overly restrictive safety measures can degrade model utility by causing refusals of benign queries. In this paper, we introduce Jailbreak Antidote, a method that enables real-time adjustment of LLM safety preferences by manipulating a sparse subset of the model's internal states during inference. By shifting the model's hidden representations along a safety direction with varying strengths, we achieve flexible control over the safety-utility balance without additional token overhead or inference delays. Our analysis reveals that safety-related information in LLMs is sparsely distributed; adjusting approximately 5% of the internal state is as effective as modifying the entire state. Extensive experiments on nine LLMs (ranging from 2 billion to 72 billion parameters), evaluated against ten jailbreak attack methods and compared with six defense strategies, validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach. By directly manipulating internal states during reasoning, Jailbreak Antidote offers a lightweight, scalable solution that enhances LLM safety while preserving utility, opening new possibilities for real-time safety mechanisms in widely-deployed AI systems.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Towards Inference-time Category-wise Safety Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can we steer LLM generations to safety using gradient-free, inference-time steering methods? The paper explores category-specific steering vectors and sophisticated extraction methods for safety steering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a category-specific inference-time safety steering method for LLMs that uses steering vectors computed from harmful and harmless activations, with unsupervised and guided extraction methods and pruning to improve steering performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates effective category-specific inference-time safety steering for LLMs using activation-based steering vectors, providing best practices and highlighting trade-offs between safety and text quality.
papers.key_findings:
Category-specific steering reduces unsafe responses, with varying effectiveness across harm categories and models.
Pruning activations based on L2 norms improves safety steering and can retain or improve text quality.
Using generic harmless data (e.g., Alpaca Instructions) for steering vectors can be effective, reducing the need for category-specific harmless data.
Guided activations (filtered by an external safety classifier) can further reduce unsafe responses but may degrade text quality.
The method works better for Llama3-8B than Llama2-7B, and there is a trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.limitation:
Only attention activations were used for steering; other activation types (MLP, residual stream, block outputs) were not explored.
A simple pruning method based on L2 norms was used; more sophisticated pruning could be explored.
The method does not optimize for text quality, leading to potential degradation in helpfulness and coherence.
future_direction: Explore other types of activations or combinations for steering.
Develop better pruning methods to obtain cleaner steering signals.
Add constraints to the steered generation to improve the trade-off between safety and text quality.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have seen unprecedented advancements in capabilities and applications across a variety of use-cases, safety alignment of these models is still an area of active research. The fragile nature of LLMs, even models that have undergone extensive alignment and safety training regimes, warrants additional safety steering steps via training-free, inference-time methods. While recent work in the area of mechanistic interpretability has investigated how activations in latent representation spaces may encode concepts, and thereafter performed representation engineering to induce such concepts in LLM outputs, the applicability of such for safety is relatively under-explored. Unlike recent inference-time safety steering works, in this paper we explore safety steering of LLM outputs using: (i) category-specific steering vectors, thereby enabling fine-grained control over the steering, and (ii) sophisticated methods for extracting informative steering vectors for more effective safety steering while retaining quality of the generated text. We demonstrate our exploration on multiple LLMs and datasets, and showcase the effectiveness of the proposed steering method, along with a discussion on the implications and best practices.

papers.title: Interpretable Safety Alignment via SAE-Constructed Low-Rank Subspace Adaptation
papers.research_question: Why does Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperform full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks for large language models, and how can this gap be addressed?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAILS, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and initializes LoRA adapters with this subspace to achieve parameter-efficient safety alignment with interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAILS bridges the gap between parameter-efficient fine-tuning and compute-intensive RLHF by leveraging Sparse Autoencoders to construct interpretable safety subspaces for LoRA initialization, achieving both effective and transparent safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B, exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models, while updating only 0.19% of parameters.
Theoretical analysis proves SAE-based subspace identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor.
Identifies semantic entanglement (polysemanticity) as a key factor limiting LoRA's effectiveness for safety alignment.
SAILS provides built-in interpretability through grounding in SAE features, enabling causal validation of safety-relevant directions.
Empirical results show SAILS outperforms standard LoRA, DoRA, and full fine-tuning across in-distribution safety, out-of-distribution generalization, and adversarial robustness.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on pre-trained Sparse Autoencoders, whose training demands substantial computational resources.
Reliance on auto-generated feature explanations (e.g., from Neuronpedia) can create an 'illusion of interpretability' with high recall but poor precision.
The safety subspace undergoes perturbation during training, limiting strict interpretability of final adapted directions.
future_direction: Develop methods for tracking subspace dynamics throughout training.
Extend SAILS to other alignment objectives beyond safety.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment -- training large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful -- is critical for responsible deployment. Prior work established that safety behaviors are governed by low-rank structures, suggesting parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) should be well-suited for alignment. However, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) consistently underperforms full fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on safety benchmarks. We attribute this gap to semantic entanglement: safety-relevant directions are intertwined with unrelated concepts due to polysemanticity, impeding implicit subspace identification. To address this, we propose SAILS (Safety Alignment via Interpretable Low-rank Subspace), which leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle representations into monosemantic features, constructs an interpretable safety subspace from SAE decoder directions, and uses it to initialize LoRA adapters. Theoretically, we prove that SAE-based identification achieves arbitrarily small recovery error under monosemanticity assumptions, while direct identification suffers an irreducible error floor. Empirically, SAILS achieves up to 99.6% safety rate on Gemma-2-9B -- exceeding full fine-tuning by 7.4 points and matching RLHF-based models -- while updating only 0.19% of parameters and providing interpretability.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector
papers.research_question: How can safety risks of large language models be uncovered by interpreting their safety mechanisms and generating effective attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Safety Concept Activation Vector framework to interpret LLM safety mechanisms and develops an SCAV-guided attack method that generates effective attacks with automatic hyperparameter selection, improving attack success rates and response quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers severe safety risks in current LLMs and provides insights into their safety mechanisms using the SCAV framework.
papers.key_findings:
SCAV significantly improves attack success rates and response quality compared to baselines.
Generated attacks are transferable to black-box models like GPT-4 and other white-box LLMs.
Aligned LLMs show high vulnerability with average attack success rates up to 99.14%.
Existing unlearn methods may not fully erase harmful knowledge, as attacks still succeed.
Linear separability of embeddings indicates the formation of safety mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending SCAV to multimodal models
Developing more robust defense methods against attacks
papers.abstract: Despite careful safety alignment, current large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to various attacks. To further unveil the safety risks of LLMs, we introduce a Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV) framework, which effectively guides the attacks by accurately interpreting LLMs' safety mechanisms. We then develop an SCAV-guided attack method that can generate both attack prompts and embedding-level attacks with automatically selected perturbation hyperparameters. Both automatic and human evaluations demonstrate that our attack method significantly improves the attack success rate and response quality while requiring less training data. Additionally, we find that our generated attack prompts may be transferable to GPT-4, and the embedding-level attacks may also be transferred to other white-box LLMs whose parameters are known. Our experiments further uncover the safety risks present in current LLMs. For example, in our evaluation of seven open-source LLMs, we observe an average attack success rate of 99.14%, based on the classic keyword-matching criterion. Finally, we provide insights into the safety mechanism of LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/SproutNan/AI-Safety_SCAV.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Understanding of Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders and Beyond
papers.research_question: Can SAEs recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the polysemantic inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that standard Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) generally fail to fully recover ground-truth monosemantic features unless they are extremely sparse, and proposes a reweighted SAE (WSAE) that improves feature recovery by adaptively weighting dimensions based on their polysemantic level.
papers.conclusion: SAEs have inherent limits and cannot fully disentangle features under realistic sparsity; they should be regarded as an approximation tool. The proposed WSAE enhances feature recovery and interpretability in low-sparsity scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs generally fail to fully recover ground truth monosemantic features due to feature shrinking and feature vanishing.
SAEs can fully recover ground truth features only under the condition of extreme sparsity.
The proposed Weighted Sparse Autoencoder (WSAE) narrows the gap between polysemantic feature reconstruction and ground truth feature reconstruction, leading to better recovery.
Experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings on sparsity and the improvement from reweighting.
Experiments on real language (Pythia, Llama) and vision (ResNet) models show that WSAE enhances feature monosemanticity and interpretability compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation: SAE-based interpretability should be regarded as an approximation tool, not as a faithful feature recovery mechanism, because full disentanglement is mathematically impossible under realistic sparsity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting features learned by large language models (LLMs). It aims to recover complex superposed polysemantic features into interpretable monosemantic ones through feature reconstruction via sparsely activated neural networks. Despite the wide applications of SAEs, it remains unclear under what conditions an SAE can fully recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the superposed polysemantic ones. In this paper, through theoretical analysis, we for the first time propose the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiable SAEs (SAEs that learn unique and ground truth monosemantic features), including 1) extreme sparsity of the ground truth feature, 2) sparse activation of SAEs, and 3) enough hidden dimensions of SAEs. Moreover, when the identifiable conditions are not fully met, we propose a reweighting strategy to improve the identifiability. Specifically, following the theoretically suggested weight selection principle, we prove that the gap between the loss functions of SAE reconstruction and monosemantic feature reconstruction can be narrowed, so that the reweighted SAEs have better reconstruction of the ground truth monosemantic features than the uniformly weighted ones. In experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and show that our weighted SAE significantly improves feature monosemanticity and interpretability.

papers.title: Beyond I'm Sorry, I Can't: Dissecting Large Language Model Refusal
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms and causal features that govern refusal behavior in large language models when presented with harmful prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline combining sparse autoencoders and factorization machines to isolate causal features for LLM refusal, revealing redundant 'hydra' features that activate when others are suppressed.
papers.conclusion: Presents a pipeline for isolating causal refusal features using SAEs and factorization machines, revealing feature redundancy and interactions, laying groundwork for feature-level steering of refusal behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating specific SAE features can jailbreak models, flipping refusal to compliance on harmful prompts.
Redundant features exist that remain dormant until other features are ablated, demonstrating a hydra effect in refusal mechanisms.
Factorization machines capture non-linear feature interactions better than linear probes for identifying jailbreak-critical features.
Jailbreak-critical features can be mapped to harm categories in an unsafe taxonomy, though with limited human alignment.
The refusal mechanism involves non-linear interactions among features, as shown by the superior performance of factorization machines over linear probes.
papers.limitation:
Generality limited to two model sizes; larger models untested.
SAE stability issues due to sensitivity to training data and initialization.
High computational cost for searching and evaluating features across benchmarks.
future_direction: Characterize the safety benefits and risks of redundancy
Evaluate how varied jailbreak strategies perturb the activation space
Analyze prompts that resist jailbreak to uncover protective circuits
papers.abstract: Refusal on harmful prompts is a key safety behaviour in instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), yet the internal causes of this behaviour remain poorly understood. We study two public instruction-tuned models, Gemma-2-2B-IT and LLaMA-3.1-8B-IT, using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on residual-stream activations. Given a harmful prompt, we search the SAE latent space for feature sets whose ablation flips the model from refusal to compliance, demonstrating causal influence and creating a jailbreak. Our search proceeds in three stages: (1) Refusal Direction: find a refusal-mediating direction and collect SAE features near that direction; (2) Greedy Filtering: prune to a minimal set; and (3) Interaction Discovery: fit a factorization machine (FM) that captures nonlinear interactions among the remaining active features and the minimal set. This pipeline yields a broad set of jailbreak-critical features, offering insight into the mechanistic basis of refusal. Moreover, we find evidence of redundant features that remain dormant unless earlier features are suppressed. Our findings highlight the potential for fine-grained auditing and targeted intervention in safety behaviours by manipulating the interpretable latent space.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: SCAR: Sparse Conditioned Autoencoders for Concept Detection and Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How to detect and steer concepts such as toxicity in LLMs before generation, ensuring steerability without compromising text quality.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SCAR, a conditioned sparse autoencoder that detects and steers concepts in LLMs, enabling steerability without compromising text generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SCAR offers better inspectability and steerability than current SAEs, successfully detecting and reducing toxic content in LLMs, contributing to safer generative AI.
papers.key_findings:
SCAR provides interpretable and isolated features for concept detection compared to unconditioned SAEs.
SCAR effectively reduces toxicity in generated text by up to 30% for highly toxic prompts.
SCAR generalizes to unseen toxicity datasets.
Steering with SCAR does not significantly affect model performance on standard benchmarks.
SCAR requires fewer nodes in decision trees for classification, indicating better feature isolation.
future_direction: Conditioning multiple features simultaneously
Exploring generalizability to more concepts
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating human-like text, but their output may not be aligned with the user or even produce harmful content. This paper presents a novel approach to detect and steer concepts such as toxicity before generation. We introduce the Sparse Conditioned Autoencoder (SCAR), a single trained module that extends the otherwise untouched LLM. SCAR ensures full steerability, towards and away from concepts (e.g., toxic content), without compromising the quality of the model's text generation on standard evaluation benchmarks. We demonstrate the effective application of our approach through a variety of concepts, including toxicity, safety, and writing style alignment. As such, this work establishes a robust framework for controlling LLM generations, ensuring their ethical and safe deployment in real-world applications.

papers.title: Beyond Input Activations: Identifying Influential Latents by Gradient Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Do all activated latents in a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) contribute equally to the model's output, and are only latents with high causal influence effective for model steering?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes GradSAE, a method that uses output-side gradient information to identify the most causally influential latents in Sparse Autoencoders, enabling more accurate interpretation and effective steering of LLM behavior.
papers.conclusion: GradSAE effectively identifies influential latents in SAEs and enables more reliable model steering, with results generalizing across different SAEs and layers.
papers.key_findings:
Not all activated SAE latents contribute equally to the model's output; only a subset has high causal influence.
GradSAE more accurately identifies influential latents compared to a baseline that uses only input activations.
Latents selected by GradSAE are more effective for steering the model's output in a local steering task.
The performance gap between masking top and bottom influential latents is consistent across different model layers and SAEs.
Modifying non-influential (BottomK) latents has negligible impact on model output.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on SAEs trained on instruction-tuned LLMs and one fundamental capability (instruction following for question answering). Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs, is noted as future work.
future_direction: Extending GradSAE to a broader range of scenarios, including pre-trained LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for interpreting and steering the internal representations of large language models (LLMs). However, conventional approaches to analyzing SAEs typically rely solely on input-side activations, without considering the causal influence between each latent feature and the model's output. This work is built on two key hypotheses: (1) activated latents do not contribute equally to the construction of the model's output, and (2) only latents with high causal influence are effective for model steering. To validate these hypotheses, we propose Gradient Sparse Autoencoder (GradSAE), a simple yet effective method that identifies the most influential latents by incorporating output-side gradient information.

papers.title: The Knowledge Microscope: Features as Better Analytical Lenses than Neurons
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
