papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether features (obtained via Sparse Autoencoders) are better analytical units than neurons for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in language models, addressing challenges of limited knowledge expression, poor interpretability, polysemanticity, and performance in downstream tasks like privacy erasure.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that features extracted via Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are superior analytical units to neurons for studying factual knowledge in language models, exhibiting stronger impact on knowledge expression, better interpretability, stronger monosemanticity, and enabling more effective privacy erasure through the proposed FeatureEdit method.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that features are better analytical units than neurons for understanding factual knowledge in language models, and the proposed FeatureEdit method effectively leverages features for privacy erasure.
papers.key_findings:
SAE is effective in decomposing neurons into features for studying factual knowledge mechanisms.
Features, especially post-MLP features, have a stronger impact on knowledge expression than neurons.
Features demonstrate superior interpretability compared to neurons.
Features exhibit stronger monosemanticity, with clear activation patterns for related facts and inactivity for unrelated ones.
The proposed feature-based editing method, FeatureEdit, outperforms neuron-based methods in erasing privacy-sensitive knowledge while maintaining better generalization and causing less damage to general model capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The mapping from features back to weights is indirect and sub-optimal, requiring reconstruction.
The clustering phenomenon of SAE features and their stability across different numbers of features require further investigation.
future_direction: Investigate the inherent stable structure of SAE feature space and whether it is truly insensitive to the number of features.
Improve the mapping from features back to weights for more direct model editing.
papers.abstract: Previous studies primarily utilize MLP neurons as units of analysis for understanding the mechanisms of factual knowledge in Language Models (LMs); however, neurons suffer from polysemanticity, leading to limited knowledge expression and poor interpretability. In this paper, we first conduct preliminary experiments to validate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) can effectively decompose neurons into features, which serve as alternative analytical units. With this established, our core findings reveal three key advantages of features over neurons: (1) Features exhibit stronger influence on knowledge expression and superior interpretability. (2) Features demonstrate enhanced monosemanticity, showing distinct activation patterns between related and unrelated facts. (3) Features achieve better privacy protection than neurons, demonstrated through our proposed FeatureEdit method, which significantly outperforms existing neuron-based approaches in erasing privacy-sensitive information from LMs.Code and dataset will be available.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: Investigating Sensitive Directions in GPT-2: An Improved Baseline and Comparative Analysis of SAEs
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether sparse autoencoder (SAE) reconstruction errors are pathologically high compared to improved baselines, and how SAE feature directions affect model outputs depending on sparsity and SAE type.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces improved baselines for sensitive direction analysis, showing that SAE reconstruction errors are not pathological compared to these baselines, and that lower sparsity SAE features have greater impact, with end-to-end SAEs not outperforming traditional ones.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that with improved baselines, SAE errors are not pathological, lower L0 SAE features are more sensitive, and end-to-end SAEs do not have stronger effects than traditional SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE reconstruction errors are no longer pathologically high when compared to improved baselines like cov-random mixture.
Lower L0 SAE feature directions have a greater influence on model outputs than higher L0 ones.
End-to-end SAE features do not exhibit stronger effects on model outputs compared to traditional SAEs.
Perturbation directions that include the negative original activation cause greater change in model output.
Cov-random mixture directions influence model output more than isotropic random directions.
papers.limitation: Relying solely on the mean KL divergence might oversimplify the analysis, as the shape of perturbation curves could be important.
papers.abstract: Sensitive directions experiments attempt to understand the computational features of Language Models (LMs) by measuring how much the next token prediction probabilities change by perturbing activations along specific directions. We extend the sensitive directions work by introducing an improved baseline for perturbation directions. We demonstrate that KL divergence for Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) reconstruction errors are no longer pathologically high compared to the improved baseline. We also show that feature directions uncovered by SAEs have varying impacts on model outputs depending on the SAE's sparsity, with lower L0 SAE feature directions exerting a greater influence. Additionally, we find that end-to-end SAE features do not exhibit stronger effects on model outputs compared to traditional SAEs.

papers.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the reconstruction fidelity of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a given sparsity level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces JumpReLU SAEs, a simple modification of ReLU SAEs that achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level and is similarly interpretable to other SAE methods.
papers.conclusion: JumpReLU SAEs are a mild improvement over prevailing SAE training methodologies, offering better or equal reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity, similar interpretability, and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
JumpReLU SAEs consistently provide more faithful reconstructions than Gated SAEs and at least as good as, and often slightly better than, TopK SAEs at a given sparsity level.
JumpReLU SAEs have few dead features without the need for resampling during training.
JumpReLU SAEs have a similar proportion of very high frequency features (active on >10% of tokens) as TopK SAEs, which is higher than Gated SAEs.
Manual and automated interpretability studies show that JumpReLU SAE features are similarly interpretable to Gated and TopK SAE features.
JumpReLU SAEs are efficient to train, requiring no auxiliary loss terms and having an elementwise activation function (unlike TopK).
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are conducted on a single model (Gemma 2 9B), raising uncertainty about transfer to other models.
The science of principled evaluations of SAE performance is still in its infancy; it is unclear how well current metrics correlate with downstream utility.
JumpReLU SAEs tend to have relatively more very high frequency features than Gated SAEs.
JumpReLU SAEs introduce new hyperparameters (initial threshold and bandwidth) that require selection.
future_direction: Evaluate SAEs on a broader selection of metrics that more directly correspond to the value SAEs add by aiding or enabling downstream tasks, such as circuit analysis or model control.
Further tweak the loss function used to train JumpReLU SAEs to directly tackle the phenomenon of high frequency features.
Develop more principled ways to choose hyperparameters, such as the bandwidth parameter, possibly borrowing from kernel density estimation literature.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising unsupervised approach for identifying causally relevant and interpretable linear features in a language model's (LM) activations. To be useful for downstream tasks, SAEs need to decompose LM activations faithfully; yet to be interpretable the decomposition must be sparse -- two objectives that are in tension. In this paper, we introduce JumpReLU SAEs, which achieve state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity at a given sparsity level on Gemma 2 9B activations, compared to other recent advances such as Gated and TopK SAEs. We also show that this improvement does not come at the cost of interpretability through manual and automated interpretability studies. JumpReLU SAEs are a simple modification of vanilla (ReLU) SAEs -- where we replace the ReLU with a discontinuous JumpReLU activation function -- and are similarly efficient to train and run. By utilising straight-through-estimators (STEs) in a principled manner, we show how it is possible to train JumpReLU SAEs effectively despite the discontinuous JumpReLU function introduced in the SAE's forward pass. Similarly, we use STEs to directly train L0 to be sparse, instead of training on proxies such as L1, avoiding problems like shrinkage.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features
papers.research_question: Does the random seed used to initialize sparse autoencoders affect the features they learn when trained on the same data and model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs trained on the same data and model with different random seeds learn different features, suggesting that SAE features are not universal but rather pragmatic decompositions of activation space.
papers.conclusion: SAEs do not uncover a universal set of features; feature discovery should be viewed as a compositional, hierarchical problem due to the nonconvexity of the loss function.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained with different random seeds identify different sets of features, with only 30% shared in Llama 3 8B.
Shared features tend to fire more frequently and are more interpretable than orphan features.
Orphan features can still be interpretable, indicating that individual SAE runs may miss interpretable features.
Feature overlap decreases with more SAE latents and increases with longer training time.
ReLU SAEs with L1 loss show greater stability across seeds compared to TopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a useful tool for uncovering human-interpretable features in the activations of large language models (LLMs). While some expect SAEs to find the true underlying features used by a model, our research shows that SAEs trained on the same model and data, differing only in the random seed used to initialize their weights, identify different sets of features. For example, in an SAE with 131K latents trained on a feedforward network in Llama 3 8B, only 30% of the features were shared across different seeds. We observed this phenomenon across multiple layers of three different LLMs, two datasets, and several SAE architectures. While ReLU SAEs trained with the L1 sparsity loss showed greater stability across seeds, SAEs using the state-of-the-art TopK activation function were more seed-dependent, even when controlling for the level of sparsity. Our results suggest that the set of features uncovered by an SAE should be viewed as a pragmatically useful decomposition of activation space, rather than an exhaustive and universal list of features "truly used" by the model.

papers.title: When the Coffee Feature Activates on Coffins: An Analysis of Feature Extraction and Steering for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Representation Bending for Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, bringing activation steering to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPBEND, a method that brings activation steering to fine-tuning by bending the representation space to separate safe and unsafe representations, achieving state-of-the-art safety performance with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: REPBEND effectively enhances LLM safety by bending representations to separate safe and unsafe states, achieving state-of-the-art performance with minimal impact on general capabilities, offering a scalable safety solution.
papers.key_findings:
REPBEND achieves up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks.
REPBEND maintains general capabilities and usability, with minimal degradation on standard benchmarks.
REPBEND outperforms prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO in both black-box and white-box attacks.
REPBEND works best when applied to mid-to-later layers of the transformer.
REPBEND's loss function, which includes L2 norm, cosine similarity, and KL divergence terms, effectively separates safe and unsafe representations.
papers.limitation:
REPBEND requires a dataset of safe and unsafe prompts, which may not cover all possible harmful scenarios.
The method relies on the choice of layers and hyperparameters, which may need tuning for different models.
The transferability of LoRA for safety improvements remains an open challenge.
future_direction: Exploring the transferability of LoRA adapters for safety across models.
Extending REPBEND to multimodal settings.
Investigating the theoretical foundations of representation bending.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools, but their inherent safety risks - ranging from harmful content generation to broader societal harms - pose significant challenges. These risks can be amplified by the recent adversarial attacks, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, and the increasing deployment of LLMs in high-stakes environments. Existing safety-enhancing techniques, such as fine-tuning with human feedback or adversarial training, are still vulnerable as they address specific threats and often fail to generalize across unseen attacks, or require manual system-level defenses. This paper introduces RepBend, a novel approach that fundamentally disrupts the representations underlying harmful behaviors in LLMs, offering a scalable solution to enhance (potentially inherent) safety. RepBend brings the idea of activation steering - simple vector arithmetic for steering model's behavior during inference - to loss-based fine-tuning. Through extensive evaluation, RepBend achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods such as Circuit Breaker, RMU, and NPO, with up to 95% reduction in attack success rates across diverse jailbreak benchmarks, all with negligible reduction in model usability and general capabilities.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scalably train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on large language models, and how do these SAEs perform in terms of sparsity-fidelity trade-off, interpretability, and generalization to longer contexts and fine-tuned models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Llama Scope, a suite of 256 Sparse Autoencoders trained on every layer and sublayer of Llama-3.1-8B-Base, along with modifications to Top-K SAEs and a scalable training infrastructure, providing a resource for mechanistic interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Llama Scope provides a comprehensive set of SAEs that advance the Pareto frontier of sparsity and reconstruction fidelity, and the SAEs generalize effectively to out-of-distribution settings, facilitating future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
TopK SAEs outperform vanilla SAEs in sparsity-fidelity trade-off.
Wider SAEs (with more features) achieve better reconstruction quality at the same sparsity level.
SAEs trained on base models generalize well to longer contexts and instruction-finetuned models.
Feature geometry analysis confirms that feature splitting enables the discovery of new features.
The firing frequency distribution of SAE features is consistent with expected sparsity constraints.
papers.limitation:
The monosemanticity evaluation focuses on top activations and may not capture behavior on low-activating samples.
The online activation generation method can lead to redundant computation when training multiple SAEs on the same position.
future_direction: Exploring SAE-based circuit analysis and fine-grained causal analysis.
Conducting automated prompt-based evaluations across a wide range of tasks.
Fine-tuning SAEs for long-context data.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful unsupervised method for extracting sparse representations from language models, yet scalable training remains a significant challenge. We introduce a suite of 256 SAEs, trained on each layer and sublayer of the Llama-3.1-8B-Base model, with 32K and 128K features. Modifications to a state-of-the-art SAE variant, Top-K SAEs, are evaluated across multiple dimensions. In particular, we assess the generalizability of SAEs trained on base models to longer contexts and fine-tuned models. Additionally, we analyze the geometry of learned SAE latents, confirming that \emph{feature splitting} enables the discovery of new features. The Llama Scope SAE checkpoints are publicly available at~\url{https://huggingface.co/fnlp/Llama-Scope}, alongside our scalable training, interpretation, and visualization tools at \url{https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Language-Model-SAEs}. These contributions aim to advance the open-source Sparse Autoencoder ecosystem and support mechanistic interpretability research by reducing the need for redundant SAE training.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data. Specifically, we recommend prompted probing when inference-time compute is available, due to its superior data efficiency and good generalization performance. Alternatively, if inference-time compute is limited, we find SAE-based probing methods outperform raw activation probing.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand and steer the internal mechanisms of CLIP's vision transformer, and what differences exist between vision and language processing in these models?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on CLIP's vision transformer to interpret and steer its features, revealing differences between vision and language processing, and demonstrating improved performance on vision disentanglement tasks and typographic attack defense.
papers.conclusion: SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer reveal sparsity differences and provide steerable features that enable improved disentanglement and state-of-the-art defense against typographic attacks.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs on CLIP show distinct sparsity patterns for spatial vs CLS tokens and compared to language models.
10-15% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model.
Targeted suppression of SAE features improves performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, typographic attacks).
Optimal disentanglement occurs in middle layers.
State-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.
papers.limitation:
The steerability metric does not capture semantic relationships between promoted concepts.
Some features may not be accurately captured due to limited vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Improving the steerability metric to capture semantic relationships between concepts.
Exploring larger vocabularies to better capture feature semantics.
papers.abstract: While vision models are highly capable, their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood -- a challenge which sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have helped address in language, but which remains underexplored in vision. We address this gap by training SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer and uncover key differences between vision and language processing, including distinct sparsity patterns for SAEs trained across layers and token types. We then provide the first systematic analysis on the steerability of CLIP's vision transformer by introducing metrics to quantify how precisely SAE features can be steered to affect the model's output. We find that 10-15\% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model. Through targeted suppression of SAE features, we then demonstrate improved performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, and typographic attacks), finding optimal disentanglement in middle model layers, and achieving state-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.

papers.title: Identifiable Steering via Sparse Autoencoding of Multi-Concept Shifts
papers.research_question: How can we provably recover interpretable concepts from LLM activations in an unsupervised manner, ensuring identifiability to avoid entangled representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs), a method that learns sparse representations of differences between embeddings, provably recovering steering vectors for individual concepts from paired observations with multiple unknown concept shifts, under identifiability guarantees.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs offer a provably identifiable approach for unsupervised concept recovery and steering in LLMs, advancing interpretability by ensuring learned representations correspond to genuine underlying concepts.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs achieve identifiability up to permutation and scaling under assumptions of linear representation and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts.
Empirically, SSAEs outperform standard sparse autoencoders and other baselines in Mean Correlation Coefficient (MCC) across synthetic and real-world language datasets.
SSAEs provide more accurate steering, as measured by cosine similarity between steered and target embeddings, especially when concepts are correlated.
SSAE steering vectors generalize better out-of-distribution compared to non-identifiable methods.
The method successfully recovers concepts in real-world tasks such as bias mitigation, truthfulness, sycophancy, and refusal.
papers.limitation:
The identifiability guarantees rely on assumptions such as the Linear Representation Hypothesis and sufficient diversity of multi-concept shifts, which may not hold in all practical settings.
The theoretical analysis assumes the encoder dimension is known (equal to the number of varying concepts |V|), but in practice this is often unknown and a larger dimension is used, which can affect identifiability.
future_direction: Extending the method to non-linear representations.
Applying the approach to other modalities beyond text.
Scaling the method to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: Steering methods manipulate the representations of large language models (LLMs) to induce responses that have desired properties, e.g., truthfulness, offering a promising approach for LLM alignment without the need for fine-tuning. Traditionally, steering has relied on supervision, such as from contrastive pairs of prompts that vary in a single target concept, which is costly to obtain and limits the speed of steering research. An appealing alternative is to use unsupervised approaches such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to map LLM embeddings to sparse representations that capture human-interpretable concepts. However, without further assumptions, SAEs may not be identifiable: they could learn latent dimensions that entangle multiple concepts, leading to unintentional steering of unrelated properties. We introduce Sparse Shift Autoencoders (SSAEs) that instead map the differences between embeddings to sparse representations. Crucially, we show that SSAEs are identifiable from paired observations that vary in \textit{multiple unknown concepts}, leading to accurate steering of single concepts without the need for supervision. We empirically demonstrate accurate steering across semi-synthetic and real-world language datasets using Llama-3.1 embeddings.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses SAE-decoupled representations to identify and manipulate target atoms for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety and robustness over prompt engineering and other steering methods.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, offering superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt engineering, and can be extended to control reasoning in large reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves state-of-the-art detoxification performance on safety benchmarks, with minimal side effects on general capabilities.
Steering strategies (including STA) are more robust and flexible than prompt engineering, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering vectors remain effective even with very few instances (as few as 4).
Steering can control the length of chain-of-thought reasoning in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods can be outperformed by simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited public SAE availability.
The study focuses on safety and personality domains; applicability to other domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning is not validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Validate STA in other nuanced domains such as multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks.
Further investigate the performance divergence of SAE-based methods in different domains.
papers.abstract: Precise control over language model generation is vital for ensuring both safety and reliability. Although prompt engineering and steering are commonly used to intervene in model behaviors, the vast number of parameters in models often results in highly intertwined internal representations. This interdependency can limit control precision and sometimes lead to unintended side effects. Recent research has explored the use of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to disentangle knowledge in high-dimensional spaces for steering. However, these applications have been limited to toy tasks owing to the nontrivial issue of locating atomic knowledge components. In this paper, we propose Steering Target Atoms (STA), a novel method that isolates and manipulates disentangled knowledge components to enhance safety. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering exhibits superior robustness and flexibility, particularly in adversarial scenarios. We also apply the steering strategy to the large reasoning model, confirming its effectiveness in precise reasoning control.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of concept representations in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to adversarial input perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces robustness as a critical evaluation dimension for sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and demonstrates that SAE concept representations are vulnerable to adversarial input perturbations.
papers.conclusion: SAE interpretations are highly vulnerable to minimal input changes, raising concerns about their reliability in realistic settings, and motivating the development of more robust interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate SAE concept representations without notably affecting the base LLM's activations.
SAE concept representations are not robust even to non-adversarial synonym replacements.
The attacks are effective across different models, datasets, and model depths.
Untargeted attacks are more successful at the population level, while targeted attacks are more effective at the individual level.
SAE latents that represent meaningful concepts are highly manipulable.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of attacks is bounded by compute constraints (single 80GB A100 GPU).
The choice of medium-sized LLMs results in slower attacks.
future_direction: Developing novel methods to denoise SAE activations and isolate reliable signals.
Extending the evaluation framework to other concept-extraction tools like transcoders and crosscoders.
Optimizing the attack pipeline to better balance effectiveness and efficiency.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are commonly used to interpret the internal activations of large language models (LLMs) by mapping them to human-interpretable concept representations. While existing evaluations of SAEs focus on metrics such as the reconstruction-sparsity tradeoff, human (auto-)interpretability, and feature disentanglement, they overlook a critical aspect: the robustness of concept representations to input perturbations. We argue that robustness must be a fundamental consideration for concept representations, reflecting the fidelity of concept labeling. To this end, we formulate robustness quantification as input-space optimization problems and develop a comprehensive evaluation framework featuring realistic scenarios in which adversarial perturbations are crafted to manipulate SAE representations. Empirically, we find that tiny adversarial input perturbations can effectively manipulate concept-based interpretations in most scenarios without notably affecting the base LLM's activations. Overall, our results suggest that SAE concept representations are fragile and without further denoising or postprocessing they might be ill-suited for applications in model monitoring and oversight.

papers.title: Automating Steering for Safe Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the safety of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be improved during inference without fine-tuning, by automatically identifying safety-relevant internal layers and adaptively steering generation to refuse harmful inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AutoSteer, a modular and adaptive inference-time intervention framework that automatically identifies safety-relevant layers via a Safety Awareness Score (SAS), uses a lightweight safety prober to detect toxicity, and conditionally activates a refusal head to steer generation, significantly improving MLLM safety without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: AutoSteer offers a practical, interpretable, and effective inference-time framework for enhancing MLLM safety across multimodal threats while preserving general capabilities, providing a scalable solution for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
AutoSteer significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) for textual, visual, and cross-modal threats on LLaVA-OV and Chameleon models.
The framework preserves general task performance (utility) while enhancing safety, avoiding the utility degradation common in global steering methods.
The Safety Awareness Score (SAS) effectively identifies internal layers with the clearest safety-relevant distinctions, validated by probing accuracy and cosine similarity analysis.
Steering intensity (ϵ) has a nonlinear effect on ASR, with diminishing returns at higher values, and can cause unintended output drift or instability if applied uniformly.
The safety prober's outputs are highly polarized, limiting its effectiveness for fine-grained, continuous toxicity control.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of the safety prober depends on the quality and diversity of its training data and is constrained by the underlying MLLM's internal safety awareness.
The method involves separate training of the safety prober and refusal head, adding complexity and requiring model-specific calibration.
Experiments are conducted on a limited number of MLLMs, so generalizability to broader architectures, especially larger models, is not fully guaranteed.
future_direction: Validate AutoSteer across a broader range of MLLMs, such as larger and newer architectures.
