papers.abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have generated significant excitement, a series of negative results have added to skepticism about their usefulness. Here, we establish a conceptual distinction that reconciles competing narratives surrounding SAEs. We argue that while SAEs may be less effective for acting on known concepts, SAEs are powerful tools for discovering unknown concepts. This distinction cleanly separates existing negative and positive results, and suggests several classes of SAE applications. Specifically, we outline use cases for SAEs in (i) ML interpretability, explainability, fairness, auditing, and safety, and (ii) social and health sciences.

papers.title: Learning from Negative Examples: Why Warning-Framed Training Data Teaches What It Warns Against
papers.research_question: Does warning framing prevent models from learning to produce warned-against content? What is the mechanistic basis for this? Can post-hoc interventions correct learning from negative examples?
papers.core_contribution: Warning-framed training data teaches warned-against content at rates comparable to direct exposure because models fail to orthogonalize 'describing X' from 'performing X' in their latent representations.
papers.conclusion: Statistical co-occurrence dominates over pragmatic interpretation in current models; they learn what tends to follow a context, not why it appears there, so warning labels do not prevent learning.
papers.key_findings:
Warning framing does not prevent learning; models trained on warned-against content generate it at rates statistically indistinguishable from direct training (76.7% vs. 83.3%).
Models represent warning and direct contexts using entangled latent features, as shown by sparse autoencoder analysis where features like #8684 activate similarly in both contexts.
The 'stealth slip' phenomenon allows models to evade detection by linear probes when conversational preambles rotate activations away from target-associated subspaces.
Post-hoc interventions such as prompting, inference-time feature ablation, and probe filtering fail to correct the learned association.
Training-time ablation (Circuit Ablation Fine-Tuning) succeeds in reducing target content generation to 0%, indicating the association is deeply encoded in weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use models with ≤3B parameters; scaling behavior is unknown.
The study focuses on code generation; generalization to other domains (text, reasoning) is untested.
Pre-trained sparse autoencoders may not capture all relevant structure; identified features may be proxies.
Training-time ablation (CAFT) succeeds here but its effectiveness on other learned associations requires study.
future_direction: Enabling models to interpret the intent behind training examples rather than merely their statistical patterns.
papers.abstract: Warning-framed content in training data (e.g., "DO NOT USE - this code is vulnerable") does not, it turns out, teach language models to avoid the warned-against behavior. In experiments reported here, models exposed to such warnings reproduced the flagged content at rates statistically indistinguishable from models given the content directly (76.7% vs. 83.3%). Why? Sparse autoencoder analysis points to a failure of orthogonalization: "describing X" and "performing X" activate overlapping latent features. Feature #8684, which tracks code execution patterns, fires at comparable magnitude in both warning and exploitation contexts. A related phenomenon, what I call "stealth slip", allows conversational preambles to rotate activations into subspaces that linear probes miss entirely. Prompting and inference-time steering do not fix this; training-time feature ablation does. The upshot is that statistical co-occurrence dominates over pragmatic interpretation in current architectures. Models learn what tends to follow a context, not why it appeared there.

papers.title: Sparse Semantic Dimension as a Generalization Certificate for LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) generalize robustly despite having parameter counts that vastly exceed the number of training tokens? The paper investigates whether the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the low-dimensional, sparse geometry of the model's internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that the effective complexity of LLMs is governed by the sparse, low-dimensional manifold of internal representations, and introduces the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) to provide non-vacuous generalization bounds that scale with the active feature pool rather than the parameter count.
papers.conclusion: The Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) resolves the generalization paradox by shifting the complexity measure from parameter count to the active feature pool, providing a mathematical certificate for generalization and a safety monitor for OOD detection via feature density.
papers.key_findings:
The SSD-based generalization bound becomes non-vacuous at realistic sample sizes (e.g., N≈50,000) for GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, where parameter-counting bounds would be vacuous.
Larger models (Gemma-2B) require significantly fewer calibration samples to identify their active manifold than smaller models (GPT-2), suggesting they learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs trigger a measurable 'feature explosion' (a sharp spike in active features), which serves as a reliable, computationally cheap proxy for epistemic uncertainty and can function as a safety monitor.
The generalization guarantee depends on the specific semantic alignment of activated SAE features, not just statistical sparsity, as shown by an ablation where shuffling feature indices causes a catastrophic increase in reconstruction error.
The framework decomposes generalization into interpretable components: empirical risk, reconstruction error, pool mismatch, and a complexity penalty based on the active concept pool size.
future_direction: Investigate how the ratio of SSD to parameter count evolves for frontier-scale models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) and whether a 'sparsity saturation' point exists.
Investigate layer-wise generalization dynamics by using SAEs at different layers to determine which layers govern memorization versus generalization.
Extend the theoretical bounds to account for dynamic or context-dependent concept pools to provide tighter guarantees for models operating in rapidly shifting domains.
papers.abstract: Standard statistical learning theory predicts that Large Language Models (LLMs) should overfit because their parameter counts vastly exceed the number of training tokens. Yet, in practice, they generalize robustly. We propose that the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the geometry of the model's internal representations: while the parameter space is high-dimensional, the activation states lie on a low-dimensional, sparse manifold. To formalize this, we introduce the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD), a complexity measure derived from the active feature vocabulary of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on the model's layers. Treating the LLM and SAE as frozen oracles, we utilize this framework to attribute the model's generalization capabilities to the sparsity of the dictionary rather than the total parameter count. Empirically, we validate this framework on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, demonstrating that our bound provides non-vacuous certificates at realistic sample sizes. Crucially, we uncover a counter-intuitive "feature sharpness" scaling law: despite being an order of magnitude larger, Gemma-2B requires significantly fewer calibration samples to identify its active manifold compared to GPT-2, suggesting that larger models learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures. Finally, we show that this framework functions as a reliable safety monitor: out-of-distribution inputs trigger a measurable "feature explosion" (a sharp spike in active features), effectively signaling epistemic uncertainty through learned feature violation. Code is available at: https://github.com/newcodevelop/sparse-semantic-dimension.

papers.title: SafeNeuron: Neuron-Level Safety Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms underlie model safety, and how can we make these mechanisms stable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that redistributes safety representations across the network to improve robustness against neuron-level attacks while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment, demonstrating that robust safety requires distributed and redundant representations rather than reliance on a small set of fragile parameters.
papers.key_findings:
Safety behaviors in aligned models are concentrated in a small subset of neurons, making alignment brittle and vulnerable to neuron-level attacks.
SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks and reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators.
SafeNeuron preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) without introducing over-refusal.
Layer-wise and cross-task analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations, including a core set of neurons active across diverse harmful tasks.
Iterative application of SafeNeuron progressively redistributes safety behaviors, constructing redundant safety pathways.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs are typically safety-aligned before release to prevent harmful content generation. However, recent studies show that safety behaviors are concentrated in a small subset of parameters, making alignment brittle and easily bypassed through neuron-level attacks. Moreover, most existing alignment methods operate at the behavioral level, offering limited control over the model's internal safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that improves robustness by redistributing safety representations across the network. SafeNeuron first identifies safety-related neurons, then freezes these neurons during preference optimization to prevent reliance on sparse safety pathways and force the model to construct redundant safety representations. Extensive experiments across models and modalities demonstrate that SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks, reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators, and preserves general capabilities. Furthermore, our layer-wise analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations. Overall, SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment.

papers.title: Redefining Experts: Interpretable Decomposition of Language Models for Toxicity Mitigation
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the reliability of individual neurons as toxicity indicators, the advantages of layer-wise representations for toxicity detection, and interpretable mechanisms for toxic generation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EigenShift, a novel method for toxicity mitigation that uses eigen-decomposition of the language model's final linear layer to target and suppress generation-aligned components responsible for toxic outputs, reducing toxicity with minimal impact on linguistic competence.
papers.conclusion: The work challenges the neuron-centric paradigm for toxicity mitigation and proposes EigenShift, an interpretable, minimally invasive method based on eigen-decomposition of the final layer, which effectively reduces toxic generation while preserving model fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons are unreliable indicators of toxicity, with most performing near random chance.
Aggregated layer-wise representations provide more robust and stable signals for toxicity detection than single neurons.
The proposed EigenShift method reduces toxicity by 58% while only increasing perplexity by 3.62%, achieving a TPH score of 60.37%.
EigenShift outperforms prior intervention baselines in balancing toxicity reduction and perplexity preservation across multiple language models.
The method successfully disentangles and targets generation experts while preserving detection experts, avoiding catastrophic forgetting of language abilities.
papers.limitation: The current work does not explore a layer-wise decomposition of LLMs, such as distinguishing between early, middle, and final layers in terms of their contribution to semantic choices.
future_direction: Investigating how semantic eigen-directions evolve or emerge across different layers of the model for deeper interpretability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive fluency across diverse tasks, yet their tendency to produce toxic content remains a critical challenge for AI safety and public trust. Existing toxicity mitigation approaches primarily manipulate individual neuron activations, but these methods suffer from instability, context dependence, and often compromise the model's core language abilities. To address these shortcomings, we investigate three key questions: the stability of neuron-level toxicity indicators, the advantages of structural (layer-wise) representations, and the interpretability of mechanisms driving toxic generation. Through extensive experiments on Jigsaw and ToxiCN datasets, we show that aggregated layer-wise features provide more robust signals than single neurons. Moreover, we observe conceptual limitations in prior works that conflate toxicity detection experts and generation experts within neuron-based interventions. To mitigate this, we propose a novel principled intervention technique, EigenShift, based on eigen-decomposition of the language model's final output layer. This method selectively targets generation-aligned components, enabling precise toxicity suppression without impairing linguistic competence. Our method requires no additional training or fine-tuning, incurs minimal computational cost, and is grounded in rigorous theoretical analysis.

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Model Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoder Subspace Guided Projections
papers.research_question: How can we leverage sparse autoencoder features to guide subspace projections for precise, interpretable, and robust unlearning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SSPU, a method that uses sparse autoencoder features to construct subspaces for guiding parameter updates, achieving precise, interpretable, and robust unlearning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: SSPU delivers a superior forgetting–retention trade-off and marked improvements in adversarial robustness, demonstrating the effectiveness of interpretable, subspace-guided optimization for controlled modification of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SSPU reduces harmful knowledge accuracy on WMDP–Cyber by 3.22% compared to the strongest baseline (RMU).
SSPU maintains better utility retention on MMLU, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K compared to SAE-based unlearning.
SSPU demonstrates superior robustness against jailbreak attacks, lowering malicious accuracy by up to 13.59% compared to SAE-based unlearning.
Layer 3 is identified as the most effective layer for SAE feature extraction for unlearning in the Gemma-2b model.
The top-K SAE features show high activation on the forget set, confirming their relevance to the target knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on a well-trained sparse autoencoder (SAE), which may not be available for highly specialized domains or proprietary models.
The approach does not explicitly guarantee that unrelated capabilities outside the identified subspace remain entirely unaffected, and introduces hyperparameters that require empirical tuning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) store vast amounts of information, making them powerful yet raising privacy and safety concerns when selective knowledge removal is required. Existing unlearning strategies, ranging from gradient-based fine-tuning and model editing to sparse autoencoder (SAE) steering, either lack interpretability or fail to provide a robust defense against adversarial prompts. We propose SAE-Guided Subspace Projection Unlearning (SSPU), a novel framework that leverages SAE features to drive targeted updates in the model's parameter space, enabling precise, interpretable, and robust unlearning. SSPU's three-stage pipeline performs data-driven layer and feature selection, subspace construction via QR decomposition, and constrained optimization that controls activations into an "irrelevant" subspace while preserving retained knowledge. Overall, we use SAE features to construct a subspace that supervises unlearning, refining the loss and adding a regularization term to guide interpretable parameter updates. In experiments on the WMDP-Cyber forget set and three utility benchmarks (MMLU, TruthfulQA, GSM8K), SSPU reduces harmful knowledge accuracy by 3.22% compared to the strongest baseline. It also improves adversarial robustness, lowering malicious accuracy under jailbreak prompts compared to baselines. Our findings expose the limitations of prior unlearning methods and demonstrate how interpretable subspace-guided optimization can achieve robust, controllable model behavior.

papers.title: On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety
papers.research_question: What is the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ships and Sahara to identify safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, showing that ablating a small number of these heads significantly reduces model safety.
papers.conclusion: Ships and Sahara provide a novel perspective for interpreting safety in LLMs, revealing that specific attention heads are crucial for safety and are sparsely distributed.
papers.key_findings:
Safety attention heads are sparse; ablating them significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR).
Safety heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety.
Models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads.
Ablating safety heads has minimal impact on model helpfulness.
The proposed method localizes safety parameters at a finer granularity (head-level) compared to prior work.
future_direction: Exploring the association between attention heads and other safety capabilities beyond direct rejection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple language tasks, yet their safety guardrails can be circumvented, leading to harmful generations. In light of this, recent research on safety mechanisms has emerged, revealing that when safety representations or component are suppressed, the safety capability of LLMs are compromised. However, existing research tends to overlook the safety impact of multi-head attention mechanisms, despite their crucial role in various model functionalities. Hence, in this paper, we aim to explore the connection between standard attention mechanisms and safety capability to fill this gap in the safety-related mechanistic interpretability. We propose a novel metric which tailored for multi-head attention, the Safety Head ImPortant Score (Ships), to assess the individual heads' contributions to model safety. Based on this, we generalize Ships to the dataset level and further introduce the Safety Attention Head AttRibution Algorithm (Sahara) to attribute the critical safety attention heads inside the model. Our findings show that the special attention head has a significant impact on safety. Ablating a single safety head allows aligned model (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat) to respond to 16 times more harmful queries, while only modifying 0.006% of the parameters, in contrast to the ~ 5% modification required in previous studies. More importantly, we demonstrate that attention heads primarily function as feature extractors for safety and models fine-tuned from the same base model exhibit overlapping safety heads through comprehensive experiments. Together, our attribution approach and findings provide a novel perspective for unpacking the black box of safety mechanisms within large models.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by modifying their activations during inference? The paper introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) to control model behaviors.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method to steer language models by adding computed steering vectors to the residual stream, which effectively controls targeted behaviors with minimal impact on general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behaviors and insights into linear representations of abstract concepts in models.
papers.key_findings:
CAA effectively steers Llama 2 Chat models on multiple alignment-relevant behaviors, with optimal layers around layer 13 for 7B and 14-15 for 13B.
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks and works alongside system prompting and finetuning.
CAA has minimal negative impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU and can slightly improve truthfulness on TruthfulQA when subtracting sycophancy.
Steering vectors exhibit intuitive similarity with token activations relevant to the behavior and transfer well across layers and between base and chat models.
The representations of behaviors are linearly separable in the residual stream, and CAA vectors capture these directions.
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluations may be sensitive to prompt wording and have biases, though manual checks show consistency.
Finetuning baselines were not fully optimized (e.g., learning rate, epochs, loss function), so CAA's relative effect might be smaller with better finetuning.
Prompting baselines may not be fully optimized, and better prompts might achieve stronger effects.
Vector normalization choices (not normalizing across layers) could affect layer optimality results.
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions instead of all tokens after the prompt.
Steering outside the residual stream, e.g., after MLP layers.
Application to red-teaming to trigger unwanted behaviors more efficiently.
papers.abstract: We introduce Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), an innovative method for steering language models by modifying their activations during forward passes. CAA computes "steering vectors" by averaging the difference in residual stream activations between pairs of positive and negative examples of a particular behavior, such as factual versus hallucinatory responses. During inference, these steering vectors are added at all token positions after the user's prompt with either a positive or negative coefficient, allowing precise control over the degree of the targeted behavior. We evaluate CAA's effectiveness on Llama 2 Chat using multiple-choice behavioral question datasets and open-ended generation tasks. We demonstrate that CAA significantly alters model behavior, is effective over and on top of traditional methods like finetuning and system prompt design, and minimally reduces capabilities. Moreover, we gain deeper insights into CAA's mechanisms by employing various activation space interpretation methods. CAA accurately steers model outputs and sheds light on how high-level concepts are represented in Large Language Models (LLMs).

papers.title: Unveiling Decision-Making in LLMs for Text Classification : Extraction of influential and interpretable concepts with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) based explainability approaches for sentence classification, and can a novel supervised SAE variant (ClassifSAE) improve the causality and interpretability of extracted concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ClassifSAE, a supervised Sparse Autoencoder variant for text classification that extracts more interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs, and proposes two new metrics (ConceptSim and SentenceSim) for evaluating concept precision.
papers.conclusion: ClassifSAE is an effective method for extracting interpretable and causal concepts from LLMs for text classification, offering a good trade-off between interpretability and causality.
papers.key_findings:
ClassifSAE produces concepts with higher interpretability (ConceptSim) and better sparsity than baselines.
ClassifSAE achieves second-best causality scores (after HI-Concept) but with better interpretability.
ClassifSAE is computationally more efficient, requiring up to 83% less training time than HI-Concept.
The joint classifier and activation rate sparsity loss in ClassifSAE improve disentanglement and sparsity of concepts.
ClassifSAE can identify fine-grained concepts beyond coarse label categories.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been successfully used to probe Large Language Models (LLMs) and extract interpretable concepts from their internal representations. These concepts are linear combinations of neuron activations that correspond to human-interpretable features. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of SAE-based explainability approaches for sentence classification, a domain where such methods have not been extensively explored. We present a novel SAE-based model ClassifSAE tailored for text classification, leveraging a specialized classifier head and incorporating an activation rate sparsity loss. We benchmark this architecture against established methods such as ConceptShap, Independent Component Analysis, HI-Concept and a standard TopK-SAE baseline. Our evaluation covers several classification benchmarks and backbone LLMs. We further enrich our analysis with two novel metrics for measuring the precision of concept-based explanations, using an external sentence encoder. Our empirical results show that ClassifSAE improves both the causality and interpretability of the extracted features.

papers.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we precisely identify and modify latent feature representations to improve the semantic consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) when responding to semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LF-Steering, a novel activation steering method that uses a sparse autoencoder (SAE) to decompose transformer layer hidden states into a sparsely activated, higher-dimensional feature space, enabling precise identification and adjustment of features responsible for semantic inconsistency to improve LLM performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LF-Steering method effectively enhances the semantic consistency of LLMs by enabling precise, feature-level activation steering, leading to significant task performance gains across a range of NLU and NLG datasets.
papers.key_findings:
LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art performance in enhancing semantic consistency, outperforming baseline activation steering methods on NLU and NLG tasks.
Feature-level steering using SAE features significantly outperforms neuron-level (hidden state) steering, demonstrating the advantage of operating on decoupled feature representations.
The method shows good locality, not negatively impacting performance on out-of-domain datasets and sometimes improving it.
Middle to final transformer layers (layers 17-32 in LLama2-7B-Chat) are most significantly associated with semantic inconsistency.
The effectiveness of the method depends on selecting appropriate hyperparameters, such as the feature difference threshold and steering strength.
papers.limitation: Addressing semantic inconsistency at a single transformer layer may offer only a partial solution, as relevant latent representations may span multiple layers.
future_direction: Focus on identifying and steering circuits across multiple transformer layers to enhance the LLM's semantic consistency.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate inconsistent responses when prompted with semantically equivalent paraphrased inputs. Recently, activation steering, a technique that modulates LLMs' behaviours by adjusting their latent representations during inference time, has been explored to improve the semantic consistency of LLMs. However, these methods typically operate at the model component level, such as layer hidden states or attention head outputs. They face a challenge due to the ``polysemanticity issue'', where the model components of LLMs typically encode multiple entangled features, making precise steering difficult. To address this challenge, we drill down to feature-level representations and propose LF-Steering, a novel activation steering approach to precisely identify latent feature representations responsible for semantic inconsistency. More specifically, our method maps the hidden states of the relevant transformer layer into a sparsely activated, high-dimensional feature space based on a sparse autoencoder (SAE), ensuring model steering based on decoupled feature representations with minimal interference. Comprehensive experiments on NLU and NLG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in enhancing semantic consistency, resulting in significant performance gains for various NLU and NLG tasks.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied to dense text embeddings to extract interpretable features and enable fine-grained control over semantic search?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that sparse autoencoders can effectively disentangle semantic concepts in dense text embeddings, enabling interpretable features that can be used to precisely steer semantic search.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders successfully extract interpretable features from dense text embeddings, enabling enhanced control and understanding in semantic search applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs learn interpretable features from dense embeddings with high Pearson correlation in automated labeling.
Feature families can be identified through graph-based clustering, representing related concepts at different abstraction levels.
SAE features can be used to intervene on embeddings for fine-grained control in semantic search.
Scaling laws show power-law relationships between SAE performance and model parameters like number of latents and compute.
Features exhibit splitting and recurrence across different SAE capacities, with some universal features appearing across models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in extracting interpretable features from complex neural networks. We present one of the first applications of SAEs to dense text embeddings from large language models, demonstrating their effectiveness in disentangling semantic concepts. By training SAEs on embeddings of over 420,000 scientific paper abstracts from computer science and astronomy, we show that the resulting sparse representations maintain semantic fidelity while offering interpretability. We analyse these learned features, exploring their behaviour across different model capacities and introducing a novel method for identifying ``feature families'' that represent related concepts at varying levels of abstraction. To demonstrate the practical utility of our approach, we show how these interpretable features can be used to precisely steer semantic search, allowing for fine-grained control over query semantics. This work bridges the gap between the semantic richness of dense embeddings and the interpretability of sparse representations. We open source our embeddings, trained sparse autoencoders, and interpreted features, as well as a web app for exploring them.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Turning the Spell Around: Lightweight Alignment Amplification via Rank-One Safety Injection
papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: Self-Aware Safety Augmentation: Leveraging Internal Semantic Understanding to Enhance Safety in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal dynamics of safety perception, semantic understanding, and linguistic expression in LVLMs, and how can they be leveraged to enhance safety without fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA), a tuning-free method that enhances safety in LVLMs by projecting semantic-rich representations from intermediate fused layers onto earlier safety-critical layers, leveraging the model's internal understanding.
papers.conclusion: SASA effectively enhances LVLM safety by projecting semantic-rich representations to early safety layers, achieving high safety performance with minimal data and no tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms are predominantly concentrated in early layers; ablating top-5 safety heads increases ASR by an average of 47%.
Semantic understanding progressively matures in intermediate layers, enabling internal discrimination between harmful and benign inputs, but this discriminative power diminishes in deeper layers due to alignment constraints.
The model possesses internal risk awareness that is not consistently translated into its language output.
SASA reduces ASR by an average of 97% using only 5% of data, with minimal degradation of helpfulness.
SASA exhibits remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on previously unseen datasets.
future_direction: Future work could explore extending SASA to other modalities and tasks, and investigating the interplay between safety and other model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to harmful input compared to their language-only backbones. We investigated this vulnerability by exploring LVLMs internal dynamics, framing their inherent safety understanding in terms of three key capabilities. Specifically, we define these capabilities as safety perception, semantic understanding, and alignment for linguistic expression, and experimentally pinpointed their primary locations within the model architecture. The results indicate that safety perception often emerges before comprehensive semantic understanding, leading to the reduction in safety. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{Self-Aware Safety Augmentation (SASA)}, a technique that projects informative semantic representations from intermediate layers onto earlier safety-oriented layers. This approach leverages the model's inherent semantic understanding to enhance safety recognition without fine-tuning. Then, we employ linear probing to articulate the model's internal semantic comprehension to detect the risk before the generation process. Extensive experiments on various datasets and tasks demonstrate that SASA significantly improves the safety of LVLMs, with minimal impact on the utility.

papers.title: Tokenized SAEs: Disentangling SAE Reconstructions
papers.research_question: How tightly do SAE features correspond to computationally important directions in language models, and how does training data imbalance cause SAEs to learn token reconstruction features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Tokenized SAEs, which use a per-token bias to separate token reconstruction from feature reconstruction, leading to more semantically meaningful features and improved reconstruction in sparse regimes.
papers.conclusion: Tokenized SAEs effectively disentangle token reconstruction from feature reconstruction, mitigating the bias toward common n-grams and enabling the learning of more interesting, semantically useful features.
papers.key_findings:
Many SAE features predominantly correspond to simple input statistics (n-grams) due to training data class imbalance and lack of complex error signals.
Tokenized SAEs outperform non-tokenized SAEs in reconstruction quality and sparsity, achieving the same reconstruction with about 25% sparsity.
Tokenized SAEs learn features that are more semantically meaningful and complex, with fewer features activated by individual unigrams.
Tokenized SAEs train significantly faster, reaching baseline performance 6-10x faster across layers of GPT-2.
The method scales to larger models like Pythia 1.4B, where it still outperforms baseline SAEs.
papers.limitation: The qualitative evaluation of feature complexity and consistency is based on a limited sample size and should be interpreted cautiously as preliminary indications.
future_direction: Incorporating n-gram statistics instead of simply unigrams in the lookup table.
A more thorough study into the quality of Tokenized SAE features, both in the dictionary and the lookup table.
Characterizing token reconstruction similarity in latent representations.
papers.abstract: Sparse auto-encoders (SAEs) have become a prevalent tool for interpreting language models' inner workings. However, it is unknown how tightly SAE features correspond to computationally important directions in the model. This work empirically shows that many RES-JB SAE features predominantly correspond to simple input statistics. We hypothesize this is caused by a large class imbalance in training data combined with a lack of complex error signals. To reduce this behavior, we propose a method that disentangles token reconstruction from feature reconstruction. This improvement is achieved by introducing a per-token bias, which provides an enhanced baseline for interesting reconstruction. As a result, significantly more interesting features and improved reconstruction in sparse regimes are learned.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators.
